and moral philosophy, and theology:
of the Mexican people: where
there are many curious things concerning
the refinements of their language,
and very delicate matters
concerning the moral
virtues.

Prologue.

All nations, however barbarous, and under whatever heaven they may have been: have
set their eyes upon the wise and the powerful, so as to be persuaded; and upon the eminent men,
for their moral virtues; and upon the skilled and the valiant, in
the exercises of war; and more upon those of their own lineage than upon those of other
nations. Of this there are so many examples among the Greeks, and Latins, Spaniards,
French, and Italians, that the books are full of this matter. This
same practice was observed in this Indian nation, and most especially among
the Mexicans: among whom the wise, virtuous and eloquent men, and the
brave, were held in high esteem. And from among these they chose their high priests,
their lords, their nobles, and their captains, regardless of how lowly their birth might be:
these men governed the republics, led the armies, and presided over the
temples. They were indeed extreme in these things: most devout toward
their gods, most zealous for their republics, very civil among themselves, yet
very cruel toward their enemies, and humane and severe toward their own people.
And I believe that through these virtues they attained empire—though it
lasted but a short while, and now they have lost it all—as will be made clear to anyone who compares
what is contained in this book with the life they now lead. The reason
for this I will not state, since it is already very clear. In this book it will become very plain
that what some rivals have claimed—that everything written in these
books, both before this one and after it, are fictions and lies—is spoken
out of passion and falsehood; for what is written in this book
could not fit within the understanding of any human being to invent, nor could any living man
have been able to invent the language found in it: and all learned Indians,
if questioned, would affirm that this language is truly that of their
ancestors and of the deeds that they themselves performed.

To the most upright Father, Friar Rodrigo de Sequera, General Commissary of all the lands of the western world, with the sole exception of Peru, Friar Bernardino de Sahagún wishes happiness in both respects.

Here, most esteemed Father, you have a work worthy of royal consideration: one that was indeed gained through fierce and prolonged struggle. Of this work, the present volume is the sixth book; there are also six others following it, which together make up the full number of twelve, gathered into four volumes. This sixth book is the greatest of all, both in size and in force: it rejoices with great exultation at having found, for itself and for its brother friars, so worthy a father — not doubting at all that, under your auspices, together with the brethren, it shall attain the highest happiness. Farewell, and may you prosper everywhere; I earnestly wish it for you.

Here begins the sixth book,
of the prayers with which they prayed
to the gods: and of Rhetoric
and Moral Philosophy,

Chapter One, on the language

O valiant lord of ours,
beneath whose wings

This is Chapter One, in which is told
the speech that came truly from the heart,
which they said when they
prayed to him who was truly their
god, namely Tezcatlipoca, or
Titlacaoan, or Yaotl, when
sickness spread, so that it might
destroy people. Those who prayed thus
were the fire priests, those who were
the guardians of the temple: thus they
declared that he was all-powerful, unseen,
untouchable: very marvelous were
their teachings, the metaphors, with which
they spoke.

O lord, our ruler, lord of
the near and the night, lord of
the wind: truly...

...we defend ourselves, and find shelter: you are invisible, and not palpable: just as the night, and the air: or I, lowly and of little worth, dare to appear before your majesty: I come to speak like a rustic, a stammerer, such will be the manner of my speech, like one who goes leaping over furrows, or walking sideways: which is a very unseemly thing.

For this reason I fear provoking your wrath against me: and instead of appeasing you, I fear angering you: but your majesty will do as is pleased with my person. O lord, who have seen fit to abandon us in these days: according to the counsel that you hold, both in heaven and in hell.

Alas, sorrow: that the wrath and indignation of your majesty has descended in these days upon us: for the great and many afflictions of your indignation have drowned and submerged us: just as stones, and lances, and arrows that have descended upon the sorrowful ones who live in this world: and this is the great pestilence with which we are afflicted, and nearly destroyed.

O valiant and all-powerful lord: alas, sorrow, that now the common people are perishing,

and consuming: great destruction,
and great havoc the pestilence is now causing
among all the people: and what is most
pitiful, is that the innocent children,
who are without fault, who understood
nothing else but to play
with little pebbles, and to
make little heaps of earth: now
they die cast aside, and
dashed against the stones, and
against the walls, (a thing most sorrowful
and pitiful to see:) for not even
those remain who do not yet know how
to walk, nor to speak: nor even those
who are still in their cradles. O Lord,
everything is being swept away — the lesser,
the middling, and the greater, the old men
and old women: and people of middle age,
men and women: none is left,

your folk, and your wealth. O

O our master, O lord of the near and the nigh:
truly you are glorified, truly you are
enriched, truly you are made joyful: and with

truly it smolders, truly it

is it then indeed true now, O lord, our master,
of the night, of the wind, O self-created one,
O owner of men: how does your
heart desire it, what is it that you wish altogether:
has your tail, your wing [your humble servant], already been given up?
Is it all, is it thus, is it only this:
will the common people simply perish entirely?

Book 6, of Rhetoric

...destroyers, and your grievous lashes, upon your poor and weak people, of little substance — just as a reed made green. What is it now, our valiant, merciful, invisible, impalpable Lord, to whose will all things obey, upon whose disposition hangs the governance of the whole world, to whom everything is subject — what is it that you have determined in your divine heart? Have you perhaps determined to abandon your people and your folk entirely? Is it true that you have determined that they should perish completely, and that there be no more memory of them in the world, and that the place where they are settled become a mountain of trees or a deserted stony wasteland? Will you perhaps permit the temples, oratories, altars, and places built for your service to be destroyed and laid waste, with no more memory of them? Is it possible that your wrath, your punishment, and the indignation of your anger are entirely unappeasable, and that it must proceed until it reaches its very end...

[Nahuatl parallel text, corresponding in content to the Spanish lament above, poses similar rhetorical questions to the deity: whether all earthly goods and possessions will come to an end; whether the waters and the mountains will remain abandoned and desolate; whether the poor and afflicted people and their towns will be utterly ruined and forgotten; whether the shelters and refuges built in devotion will likewise perish without remedy; whether the suffering and anguish of the heart will never cease nor be consoled; whether what has been foretold concerning us and the land of the dead is true, and whether there is no longer any remedy or comfort anywhere; whether, even now, in this very darkness, nothing can be done to turn aside the ruin and devastation that threatens, and whether, wherever one turns, there is no place of safety upon the earth, for already the darkness has fallen and so it must be.]

of our destruction, it is already thus
determined in your divine
counsel: that no mercy is to be shown
to us, nor are you to have pity
on us? but rather that the arrows
of your fury are to finish us off, in our
total destruction and perdition? Is it
possible that this scourge and this punishment
is not given to us for our correction
and amendment, but for total destruction
and desolation? And that the sun will
shine on us no more?
but that we shall remain in perpetual darkness
and in eternal silence? And that never
again will you look upon us with eyes
of mercy, neither a little, nor much?
In this way do you wish to destroy the
wretched sick: who cannot
turn themselves from one side to the other: nor
have a moment's rest; and they
have their mouths and teeth full of earth
and tartar: it is a great sorrow to say that already
we are all in darkness, and there is no sense
nor feeling, to help one another:
nor to look after one another: all

In truth it happens that because of their fathers and
mothers having died, and having left them orphaned
and abandoned, without any shelter,
they suffer for the sins of their parents. O
our lord, all-pious, and merciful,
and our refuge: granted that your wrath, and your
indignation, and your arrows, and stones, have
gravely wounded this poor people:
let this be a punishment, as from a father or mother,
who punish their children, pulling them
by the ears, and pinching them under the
arms, whipping them with nettles, and pouring
over them very cold water: and
all this is done so that they may amend
their youthful faults and childish ways: well, it is
thus, that your punishment and your
indignation has taken hold, and gloriously
prevailed over these your servants,
over this poor people: just as
the drops of water, which after having
rained upon the trees and green canes,
touched by the wind, fall upon those
who are beneath the trees or canes.
O most humane lord, well you know that
the common people are like children, who
after having been whipped and punished,
weep and sob, and repent
of what they have done: perhaps now this
poor people, because of your punishment,
weep and sigh, and reproach themselves,
and are murmuring among themselves,
in your presence they accuse themselves, and denounce
their own evil deeds, and punish themselves for
them. Our most humane lord, most
pious, most noble, most precious: let
the punishment already given suffice, and let them be given a
term in which to amend themselves: let them not be
finished off here, but rather another time,
when they no longer
amend themselves: forgive them, and overlook
their faults: let now your wrath and your

[Nahuatl text continues in parallel, containing related ritual/petitionary language addressing "Tlacatle, totecoe" (O lord, O our lord), invoking mercy upon the little ones (piltontli, tonetontli), speaking of punishment, suffering, and the possibility of death (mjquiztli) and the lord of the underworld (mjctlan tecutli), corresponding thematically to the Spanish text on the left.]

And philosophy

...anger: gather it now within your breast, so that it may do no more harm; rest now, and let your rage and your anger subside. For in truth no one can escape death, nor flee from it to any place; we all owe tribute to death, and we are her vassals, as many as live in the world; and this tribute all pay to death. No one will escape following death, for she is your messenger, sent at whatever hour she is dispatched; for this death is hungry and thirsty to devour all there are in the world, and she is so powerful that no one can escape her; then all will be punished according to their deeds.

O most merciful Lord, at least have pity, and have mercy upon the children who lie in their cradles, and upon the children who do not yet know how to walk, who have no other occupation but to play with little pebbles and make small piles of earth. Have mercy also, Lord, upon the most wretched poor, who have nothing to eat, nor anything to cover themselves with, nor anything to sleep on; who do not know what a good day is; all their days pass in pain, affliction, and sadness.

It would not be fitting, Lord, that you should forget to have mercy on the soldiers and men of war, whom at some time you will need; and it is better that, dying in war, they go to the house of the Sun, and there be given food and drink, than that they die of pestilence and go to hell.

O most valiant Lord, protector of all, and lord of the earth, and governor of the world, and lord of all: let the time of punishment that you have already carried out be enough, and let there now be respite and contentment.

Moral (teaching)                                                  fo. 4

[The Nahuatl text parallels the Spanish composition above, a solemn prayer addressed to the deity (Tezcatlipoca/Totecue, "Our Lord"), speaking of how people live afflicted, suffering, and consumed by misery and pain; invoking the deity's mercy upon the poor, the suffering, and the fallen warriors — those whose bodies and flesh are worn by constant hunger and sorrow. It asks whether the deity wishes to call upon the eagle and the jaguar (symbols of warriors) to go to the house of the Sun, to be given drink and sustenance there in the realm of the dead and the heavens. It beseeches the Lord, "the ever-present," "owner of the near and the far," "creator of mankind," that this much punishment may now suffice, asking for his compassion and tenderness.]

Let this smoke and this mist of your anger now cease, O lord: let this burning fire and the blaze of your wrath now be extinguished: let serenity and clarity come: let the little birds of your people now begin to sing, and to warble to the sun: grant them a calm time, in which they may call upon you, and make prayer to your majesty, and may know you. O our lord, most valiant, most merciful, most noble: this little have I said before your majesty: and I have nothing more to say, except to prostrate myself, and cast myself at your feet: asking forgiveness for the faults I have committed in my prayer: for certainly I would not wish to remain in the disgrace of your majesty: and I have nothing more to say.

This is a prayer of the priests (satraps), in which they confess to him as lord of riches, rest, and contentment,

O our most valiant lord,
most humane, protector: you are the
one who gives us life, and you are invisible,
and impalpable, lord of all,
and lord of battles: here I present
myself before your majesty, for
you are protector and defender: here I

to your majesty, because of the need
that the poor common people suffer, and
those of low estate, and of little wealth in

discretion: that when they lie down at
night, they have nothing: nor likewise when
they rise in the morning: the night passes for them
and the day in great poverty. Let
your majesty know: that your vassals
and servants suffer great poverty: so
much that it cannot be exaggerated; rather
their poverty and abandonment are very great.
The men have no cloak
with which to cover themselves, nor do the women
have any garments with which they
may wrap and cover their flesh: only
some rags, torn
all over: and that the wind and the cold

O lord of the battle:
now indeed before your presence
I come to kneel, before your presence

heart, with all my words I
call upon you, I entreat you: concerning
him, concerning the tail and the wing [the lowly one],
the poor wretch who knows not how
to live, who merely lives aimlessly, who merely sleeps,
who merely idles about: he who goes about expelled
from your compassion, from your mercy:
perhaps you will take him up, you will receive him:
perhaps he suffers, perhaps he labors
here, the common man, there

through the mountains and wastelands

bodies: and the children that you have given
them, because of the misery in which they are raised:
for lack of food, and having nothing
to cover themselves with: their faces
turn yellow, and their whole body
becomes the color of earth, and they go about
trembling with cold, wearing some rag:
such poor souls, instead of a blanket
tied around the neck, and other similar things:
the women tied about the hips:
and they go about with their bellies stuck

and full of sadness, all misfortune

our most humane lord, invisible,

lord: in whose power it is to give
all contentment and relief, and sweetness
and softness, and riches, and prosperity:
for you alone are the lord of all these
goods: I beg you to have mercy
on them, for they are your servants: I beg

[The Nahuatl text is a parallel version of the same prayer given above, addressed to the god (Tezcatlipoca) on behalf of the poor and suffering. It describes the wretched, trembling, hungry, and ragged poor, their bodies wasted and weak, weeping and sighing from misfortune, finding only slight comfort by the fire. It calls upon the invisible and impalpable lord, the night, the wind, to have mercy upon his afflicted creatures, to acknowledge and console the poor who cry out and seek him in their affliction, and to grant them warmth, gentleness, sweetness, delight, and prosperity, since he alone possesses the power to grant such blessings and is beseeched to show compassion upon those who are his servants.]

may experience a little of your
tenderness and kindness, and of your
sweetness and gentleness: for in truth
they have great need and great
hardship: I beg you that you raise up
their head with your favor and aid:
I beg you, be pleased that they
have some days of prosperity
and rest: I beg you be pleased
that they have some days of
prosperity and rest: I beg you
that they have some time
in which their flesh and their bones
may receive some recreation and
relief: be pleased, lord, that
they sleep and rest in peace:
I beg you to grant them prosperous
and peaceful days of life: once

take it away, and hide, and conceal

days: as one enjoys a fragrant
and beautiful flower, which in a
short time withers. And this, when
the favors you have granted them
become for them a cause of pride and
presumption and arrogance, and
with them they become bold, presumptuous,
and insolent: then you may give those
mercies to the sad, the sorrowful, and...

[Parallel Nahuatl text — a ritual prayer addressed to the lord, asking that the person be allowed a little rest and ease, that his body and flesh and bones receive relief, that he sleep and be refreshed for a short time, like a flower that is enjoyed briefly before it withers; and that if these favors should cause him to become proud or boastful, they may then be withdrawn and given instead to the poor, the afflicted, and the suffering.]

And philosophy

...the anguished, the poor, and the needy: who are humble and obedient, and serviceable, and familiar in your house: and perform your service with great humility and diligence: and give you their heart most truly. And if this people, N., for whom I beg and beseech you to do good: they will not recognize the good you have given them, you will take the good away, and you will cast upon them the curse, so that every evil may come upon them, so that they may be poor, needy, maimed, lame, blind, and deaf: and then they will be frightened, seeing the good they had, and how it has ceased: and then they will call upon you, and take refuge in you.
